description: Small two person team, creating a lunar outpost game. Striving for global nominee
summary:
Project Sol: Mars Exploration is a browser-based educational survival game where players control a solo astronaut maintaining a scientific outpost on Mars. Players manage electricity, oxygen, water, and food, grow crops, operate a battery-powered rover, communicate with Earth, and explore the Martian environment to recover equipment and scientific data.

The game uses real NASA research and measurements to model Martian time, solar energy, atmospheric dust, temperature, life-support requirements, crop growth, and communication delays. Its landing-site map also incorporates authentic NASA terrain data from Arcadia Planitia.

When a dust storm reduces solar production and damages equipment, players must prioritize essential systems, clean solar panels, or recover replacement parts from a nearby wreck. Their decisions directly affect the survival of the mission.

Project Sol transforms real space science into an interactive learning experience, helping children understand how engineering, resource management, and scientific knowledge are connected to survival on Mars.
details:
Project Sol: Mars Exploration is a browser-based educational survival and exploration game designed for children aged 7–12. Players take control of a solo astronaut stationed at a pre-established Martian research outpost, where they must maintain essential systems, investigate the planet, and complete scientific assignments while managing limited resources.

The outpost contains interconnected electrical, life-support, agricultural, and communications systems. Players allocate electricity between oxygen production, water recycling, irrigation, heating, cooling, equipment maintenance, and communications. Solar generation changes throughout the Martian day and depends on seasonal conditions, atmospheric dust, and panel condition. Batteries store excess energy and supply essential equipment when solar production becomes insufficient.

The simulation incorporates published NASA measurements and research rather than relying entirely on arbitrary gameplay values. NASA data informs the Martian clock, solar generation, dust-storm attenuation, equipment soiling, habitat heating, astronaut oxygen and food requirements, water-recycling efficiency, crop-growth durations, and Earth–Mars communication delays. The landing-site map uses NASA Mars Trek terrain imagery of Arcadia Planitia, providing a direct connection to real Martian geography.

Environmental events create meaningful engineering challenges. During a dust storm, reduced sunlight decreases solar output while accumulated dust can continue limiting generation after the storm ends. Players must balance energy consumption, maintain essential equipment, clean affected solar panels, or investigate a nearby wreck to recover a replacement panel. Charging the rover also draws energy from the outpost, creating a trade-off between exploration and survival.

The greenhouse allows players to plant, grow, and harvest crops while managing food supplies. Time continues advancing during sleep, affecting resource consumption, battery reserves, and crop development. Communications require satellite alignment and account for the significant signal delay between Earth and Mars. These systems encourage players to plan ahead rather than react only when resources become critical.

Scientific exploration provides another part of the experience. Players travel across the Martian surface, investigate equipment, and recover research data connected to real space-exploration history. This connects scientific knowledge with practical engineering decisions and demonstrates how previous discoveries can inform future missions.

Project Sol includes a mission progression system with success and failure outcomes. Starting or retrying a mission restores the initial scenario, allowing players to experiment with different decisions and learn from their mistakes.

The game was developed using Unity 6 and C#, incorporating 2D environments, animations, physics, environmental lighting, interactive interfaces, and simulation systems. It is exported using WebGL, allowing players to experience the mission directly in a desktop browser. AI tools assisted with development and artwork creation, and AI-generated visual assets are identified within the game.

Although the simulation uses authentic NASA reference data, certain equipment specifications, environmental scenarios, and gameplay events remain simplified to make the experience understandable and engaging for younger audiences.

Our objective is to make space science more accessible by turning scientific facts into interactive challenges. Instead of simply learning that Mars has a harsh environment, players experience how that environment affects technology, survival, and exploration. Project Sol encourages scientific curiosity, problem-solving, and systems thinking by allowing children to observe the consequences of their own decisions.
